patches.name: JSON Array
patches.summary: Builds a JSON array from a list of values, such as tab titles or ids, to read by position or send as data.
patches.docs:
## How it works
A JSON Array collects several values into one ordered list, the kind of data a server sends or expects.

- **Item 0**, **Item 1**, and so on are the values, in order. Item 0 becomes the first element. Change the number of items to add or remove ports.
- **Array** is the finished list. It updates on the same frame any item changes.
- Change the patch's type to fill the items with text, numbers, colors, points, JSON, and more. Colors become `"#RRGGBBAA"` text and points become `[x, y]` lists.

## Tips
- Read one element back with Value at Index, and count elements with Array Count.
- Choosing one of a few values by number? Option Picker does that without JSON.
- Set the type to JSON to mix kinds of values, or to nest arrays and objects built by other patches.

## Coming from Origami
Item ports have names and a shared type, so you don't need a Splitter in front of each one.
patches.behavior:
Stateless.

Helper `toJson(v)`: a runtime Color `{ r, g, b, a }` becomes `formatColor(v)` ("#RRGGBBAA"); a non-finite number becomes 0 (warn once per restart through `ctx.services.log("warn", …)`); `undefined` becomes `null`; arrays and plain objects map recursively; media references (`{ assetId }` or `{ url }`) stay as objects so upload bodies can carry them; everything else passes through. Vectors are already `number[]`.

Each frame:
```
const n = Math.max(1, ctx.inputCount); // number of item ports
const array = [];
for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) array.push(toJson(ctx.input(`item${i}`)));
ctx.output("array", array);
```

- Length: always the number of item ports, whether or not each port is connected. An unconnected item contributes its literal or the variant's zero value (0, "", `"#00000000"`, `[0, 0]`, or `null`).
- Output identity: build a new array every frame; never mutate an array an upstream patch produced. Downstream patches compare by value, not identity.
- Frame 0: evaluates with authored values; no special case.
- Loops: evaluates once per loop index. A loop on any item gives a loop of arrays (longest input wins, shorter loops wrap, scalars broadcast). It does not gather a loop into one array; that's Loop to Array.
- Retargeting: changing the type re-coerces every item on the next evaluation; there is no state to reset.
- Edge cases: never emits NaN or ±Infinity inside the array. JSON-typed items are copied by reference into the new array (treat them as immutable).
- Muted: outputs `[]`, since no input has the JSON type to pass through.
- Coming from Origami: Origami's JSON Array starts with 2 unnamed, untyped ports whose element types come from upstream Splitters. Importers set `typeParam` to `json` and map ports in order to `item0…`. The legacy doc name was Array Builder.

outputs.name: Array
outputs.description: The items as one JSON array, in port order: Item 0 is the first element.

variadic.name: Item
variadic.description: The value stored at this position in the array, counted from 0.

commonMistakes: Value at Index shows the wrong item: positions count from 0, so the first item is Item 0. Subtract 1 from a count that starts at 1.
A loop wired into one item gives many arrays instead of one: JSON Array evaluates once per loop index. Use Loop to Array to turn a whole loop into an array.
Text items show up as numbers or 0: the patch is still set to Number. Change its type to Text before typing words.

patches.name: JSON Object
patches.summary: Builds a JSON object with one named value, like {"name": "Ada"}, for request bodies, headers, and nested data.
patches.docs:
## How it works
A JSON object stores values by name. This patch makes an object with exactly one entry.

- **Key** is the entry's name. Capital letters and spaces count.
- **Value** is what the key holds. Change the patch's type to store text, numbers, booleans, colors, points, JSON, or media.
- **Object** is the result, updated on the same frame Key or Value changes. When Key is empty, Object is `{}`.

Colors become `"#RRGGBBAA"` text and points become `[x, y]` lists, so the data reads cleanly as text.

## Tips
- Add more entries with Set Value for Key, or merge several objects with Object Join.
- Set the type to JSON to nest another object or an array inside this one.
- Build request headers such as `Authorization` with a Text value.
patches.behavior:
Stateless.

Helper `toJson(v)`: a runtime Color becomes `formatColor(v)` ("#RRGGBBAA"); a non-finite number becomes 0 (warn once per restart); `undefined` becomes `null`; arrays and plain objects map recursively; media references (`{ assetId }` or `{ url }`) stay as objects; everything else passes through.

Each frame:
```
const key = ctx.input<string>("key");
ctx.output("object", key === "" ? {} : { [key]: toJson(ctx.input("value")) });
```

- Keys: used exactly as typed, case-sensitive, with no trimming and no path syntax ("a.b" is one key). Build the object with a null-prototype-safe assignment (`Object.defineProperty` or a `Map` converted to an object) so keys such as `__proto__` are stored as ordinary keys.
- Empty key: outputs `{}`, so a patch whose Key isn't filled in yet adds nothing downstream.
- Output identity: a new object every frame; never mutate the value input.
- Frame 0: evaluates with authored values; no special case.
- Loops: evaluates once per loop index. Looped Key and Value zip into a loop of one-entry objects (longest wins, shorter loops wrap, scalars broadcast). Gathering them into one object needs Object Join or a script.
- Retargeting: changing the type re-coerces Value on the next evaluation.
- Edge cases: never stores NaN or ±Infinity. A `null` JSON value is stored as `null`, not dropped.
- Muted: outputs `{}` (Key is text and Value may not be JSON, so nothing passes through).
- Coming from Origami: same ports (Key, Value, Object). Origami's Value type is chosen by right-click and its default is undocumented; Sonobe defaults to Number 0. Origami doesn't document the empty-key case.

inputs.name: Key
inputs.description: The entry's name, used exactly as typed; empty text gives an empty object.

inputs.name: Value
inputs.description: The value stored under Key. Its type follows the patch's type.

outputs.name: Object
outputs.description: A JSON object with one entry: Key set to Value.

commonMistakes: The object only ever has one entry: JSON Object holds a single key. Chain Set Value for Key after it, or join several objects with Object Join.
The server ignores the value: keys are case-sensitive and exact, so "userId" isn't "userid ". Match the key the API expects character for character.
A number arrives as text, or the other way around: the patch type decides how Value is stored. Set the type to Number for 42 and to Text for "42".

patches.name: Value at Index
patches.summary: Reads one element of a JSON array by its position, counted from 0, like the first search result.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Value at Index picks one element out of a JSON array, the way `list[2]` does in code.

- **Array** is the list to read from.
- **Index** is the element's position, counted from 0: 0 is the first element.
- **Value** is that element. Change the patch's type to read it as text, a number, a color, a point, an image, or JSON.
- **Found** is true when the position exists. When it doesn't (past the end, negative, or Array isn't an array), Value is empty: 0, empty text, a transparent color, or nothing.

The patch reads values best effort: the text "12" reads as the number 12, `"#FF3B30"` reads as a color, and `[x, y]` or `{"x": …, "y": …}` reads as a point.

## Tips
- To show every element, use Loop Over Array instead of one Value at Index per element.
- For nested data such as `results.0.title`, Value at Path does several steps at once.
- Wire Found into a layer's Enabled to hide a placeholder when there's nothing to show.

inputs.name: Array
inputs.description: The JSON array to read from.

inputs.name: Index
inputs.description: The element's position, counted from 0; negative or past-the-end positions output an empty Value.

outputs.name: Value
outputs.description: The element at Index, read as the patch's type; empty when Found is false.

outputs.name: Found
outputs.description: True when Array is an array and Index is one of its positions.

commonMistakes: It shows the second item instead of the first: positions count from 0. Use Index 0 for the first element.
Value is 0 or empty even though the data is there: the element is an object, not a number or text. Set the type to JSON and read the field with Value for Key, or use Value at Path.
Nothing shows when the prototype starts: the request hasn't finished, so Array is still empty. Use Found or the request's Loading to show a placeholder.

patch results valueForKey object←search.result key="results"

patches.name: Value for Key
patches.summary: Reads one named field from a JSON object, such as a product's name or price.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Value for Key reads one entry of a JSON object by its name, the way `item.name` does in code.

- **Object** is the JSON object to read from, such as a network response or one item from Loop Over Array.
- **Key** is the entry's name. It must match exactly, including capital letters and spaces.
- **Value** is the entry's value. Change the patch's type to read it as text, a number, a boolean, a color, a point, an image, or JSON.
- **Found** is true when Object has that key. Otherwise Value is empty: 0, empty text, a transparent color, or nothing.

Reading is best effort: the text "4.5" reads as the number 4.5, and a URL reads as an image.

## Tips
- Keep the type at JSON when the value is another object or an array you want to keep reading.
- For several steps such as `user.address.city`, Value at Path is shorter than a chain of these.
- Not sure which keys exist? Get Keys lists them, and JSON to Text shows the whole object.

inputs.name: Object
inputs.description: The JSON object to read from.

inputs.name: Key
inputs.description: The name of the entry to read, matched exactly, including capital letters and spaces.

outputs.name: Value
outputs.description: The value stored under Key, read as the patch's type; empty when Found is false.

outputs.name: Found
outputs.description: True when Object is a JSON object that contains Key.

commonMistakes: Value stays empty: the key doesn't match exactly. "Name" and "name" are different keys; check the data with JSON to Text.
The value you need is one level deeper, so Value is an object instead of text: the field is nested. Chain another Value for Key, or use Value at Path with a path like `user.name`.
A price shows as 0: the patch type is Text or JSON wired into a number property that can't read it, or the price is text like "$4". Set the type to Number and make sure the data holds a plain number.

examples.title: List products from a JSON file
examples.description: Loop Over Array turns the array into a loop, so each Value for Key reads one field per row.

  layer row_price text "Price" text←prices.value

patch names valueForKey<text> object←rows.items key="name"
patch prices valueForKey<text> object←rows.items key="price"

patches.name: Value at Path
patches.summary: Reads a value deep inside JSON with a dot path like results.0.title, including every match with * or a .. search.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Value at Path walks through nested JSON one step at a time. **Path** is a list of steps separated by dots.

- A word such as `title` reads that key from an object.
- A whole number such as `0` reads that position from an array, counted from 0.
- `*` reads every child and gives back an array: `books.*.title` lists every book's title.
- Starting with `..` searches everything: `..title` finds every `title` key at any depth, in the order they appear.
- An empty Path gives back the whole Object.

**Value** is the result, read as the patch's type. **Found** is true when the path leads somewhere. When it doesn't, Value is empty: 0, empty text, a transparent color, or nothing.

## Tips
- Paths with `*` or `..` always give an array. Feed it into Loop Over Array to show one row per match.
- Keys that contain dots can't be written in a path; use Value for Key for those.
- Build a path from a loop index with Format Number or Add, such as `items.3.name`.

inputs.name: Object
inputs.description: The JSON object or array to read from.

inputs.name: Path
inputs.description: Steps separated by dots: keys, positions from 0, * for every child, or a leading .. to search everything. Empty returns the whole Object.

outputs.name: Value
outputs.description: What the path leads to, read as the patch's type; an array for * and .. paths, and empty when Found is false.

outputs.name: Found
outputs.description: True when every step of the path resolved.

commonMistakes: Value is empty for `results[0].title`: paths use dots only. Write `results.0.title`.
Text shows brackets and quotes: a path with * or .. returns an array. Feed it into Loop Over Array, or use a position such as `books.0.title` for one value.
Nothing is found even though the key looks right: spaces and capitals count, and a path like `user.` has an empty step. Remove stray spaces and trailing dots.

patches.name: Set Value for Key
patches.summary: Adds or replaces one named field in a JSON object and outputs the updated copy.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Set Value for Key takes a JSON object and gives back a copy with one entry changed. The original object stays as it was for any other patch reading it.

- **Object** is the object to start from.
- **Key** is the entry to set. If Object already has it, its value is replaced in the same position; otherwise the entry is added at the end.
- **Value** is the new value. Change the patch's type to store text, numbers, booleans, colors, points, JSON, or media.
- **Output** is the updated object, on the same frame any input changes.

While Key is empty, Output is Object unchanged, so you can insert the patch into a chain safely.

## Tips
- Chain several of these to build a request body field by field.
- To combine whole objects at once, use Object Join.
- Keys are top-level only: "user.name" is one key with a dot in it, not a nested field.
patches.behavior:
Stateless.

Helper `toJson(v)`: a runtime Color becomes "#RRGGBBAA"; a non-finite number becomes 0 (warn once per restart); `undefined` becomes `null`; arrays and plain objects map recursively; media references stay as objects; everything else passes through.

Each frame:
```
const object = ctx.input("object");
const key = ctx.input<string>("key");
const base = isPlainObject(object) ? object : {};
if (object !== null && !isPlainObject(object)) warnOnce("Object isn't a JSON object, so Set Value for Key starts from {}");
if (key === "") { ctx.output("output", base); return; }
const out = shallowCopy(base);                  // same key order
defineOwn(out, key, toJson(ctx.input("value"))); // replaces in place, or appends at the end
ctx.output("output", out);
```

- Immutability: never mutate the incoming object; copy it shallowly each frame. Nested objects are shared by reference and must be treated as immutable downstream.
- Keys: exact and case-sensitive, no path syntax. Store with an own-property definition so `__proto__` becomes an ordinary key.
- Order: replacing keeps the key's position; a new key goes last (JavaScript key order still lists whole-number keys first).
- Non-objects: `null` starts from `{}` silently; arrays, text, numbers, and booleans start from `{}` and warn once per restart per loop index through `ctx.services.log("warn", …)`.
- Frame 0: evaluates with authored values; no special case.
- Loops: evaluates once per loop index. A loop of objects (such as items from Loop Over Array) with one Key and Value sets the field on every item; looped Values give each item its own value. Longest input wins, shorter loops wrap, scalars broadcast.
- Retargeting: changing the type re-coerces Value on the next evaluation.
- Restart and dispose: restart clears the warn-once flags. Nothing to release.
- Coming from Origami: same inputs. Origami's output is also named Object; Sonobe names it Output because the input already uses that key. Origami doesn't document empty keys or non-object inputs.

inputs.name: Object
inputs.description: The JSON object to start from; it isn't changed for other patches.

inputs.name: Key
inputs.description: The entry to add or replace, matched exactly; empty passes Object through unchanged.

inputs.name: Value
inputs.description: The new value for Key. Its type follows the patch's type.

outputs.name: Output
outputs.description: A copy of Object with Key set to Value.

commonMistakes: The change never reaches the original data: Set Value for Key makes a copy. Read from its Output downstream instead of from the original object.
A nested field isn't updated and a new key with a dot appears instead: keys are top-level only. Read the inner object with Value for Key, set the field on it, then set it back on the outer object.
The value disappears on the next frame after a tap: this patch has no memory. Store the value in a Switch, Counter, or Sample and Hold and wire that into Value.

patches.name: Get Keys
patches.summary: Lists the names of every entry in a JSON object as an array of text, so you can show or loop over them.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Get Keys looks at a JSON object and outputs the names of its top-level entries.

- **Object** is the object to inspect.
- **Keys** is a JSON array of text, one per entry. Nested objects aren't searched.
- Keys come out in the order they appear in the object, except that keys made only of digits (such as "2024") come first, smallest to largest.
- Anything that isn't an object gives an empty array.

## Tips
- Loop over an object: Get Keys, then Loop Over Array, then Value for Key with the looped key and the same object.
- Need alphabetical order? Put Array Sort after it.
- Count the entries with Array Count.

inputs.name: Object
inputs.description: The JSON object whose entry names you want.

outputs.name: Keys
outputs.description: A JSON array of the object's top-level key names, as text.

commonMistakes: Keys is empty for your data: the value is an array, not an object. Read one item with Value at Index first, or use Array Count for the length.
The order looks shuffled: keys made of digits come first, smallest to largest. Put Array Sort after Get Keys, or keep the order in an array instead of an object.

patches.name: Object Join
patches.summary: Merges several JSON objects into one, with later objects overwriting keys that earlier ones already have.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Object Join combines the entries of several JSON objects into one object.

- **Object 1**, **Object 2**, and so on are merged in order. Change the number of inputs to add more.
- When two objects have the same key, the later object's value wins. The key keeps the position where it first appeared.
- The merge is shallow: if both objects hold a nested object under the same key, the later nested object replaces the earlier one completely.
- Inputs that aren't objects are skipped.
- **Object** is the merged result, updated on the same frame any input changes.

## Tips
- Put defaults in Object 1 and overrides in Object 2.
- Build request headers from separate JSON Object patches, such as `Content-Type` and `Authorization`, then join them.
- To change a single key, Set Value for Key is simpler.

outputs.name: Object
outputs.description: One object holding every entry from the inputs; for duplicate keys, the later input's value.

variadic.name: Object
variadic.description: An object to merge; its keys overwrite the same keys from earlier inputs.

commonMistakes: Your override doesn't take effect: it's in an earlier input, and later inputs win. Put defaults first and overrides last.
A nested setting loses its other fields: the merge is shallow, so a nested object is replaced, not combined. Join the nested objects separately, then set the result back with Set Value for Key.

patches.name: Array Append
patches.summary: Adds an item to the end of a JSON array each time it gets a pulse, remembering everything added so far.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Array Append keeps a growing list. Each pulse (a signal that lasts one frame) on **Append** adds the current **Item** to the end.

- **Array** is the starting list. Leave it empty to start from nothing.
- **Item** is what gets added. Its value is captured at the moment of the pulse; changing it later doesn't change items already added.
- **Append** adds one item per pulse.
- **Reset** removes everything you appended and goes back to Array.
- **Output** is Array followed by every appended item.

When Array itself changes, such as new data arriving, the appended items are cleared and the list starts again from the new Array. Restarting the prototype also clears them.

Change the patch's type to append text, numbers, colors, points, JSON, and more.

## Tips
- Count the list with Array Count, or show it with Loop Over Array.
- To add a whole array at once, use Array Join.
- The list holds up to 10,000 appended items.

inputs.name: Array
inputs.description: The starting list; when it changes, previously appended items are cleared.

inputs.name: Item
inputs.description: The value to add, captured on the frame Append fires. Its type follows the patch's type.

inputs.name: Append
inputs.description: Pulse to add Item to the end of the list.

inputs.name: Reset
inputs.description: Pulse to remove every appended item and go back to Array.

The list only ever has one item: Append is wired to a state such as Down that stays on. A held state appends once; wire the Tap pulse so each tap counts.
Items vanish when the prototype restarts: appended items live only while the prototype runs. Put permanent items in Array instead.

patches.name: Array Count
patches.summary: Counts how many elements a JSON array has, such as the number of search results or items in a cart.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Array Count outputs how many elements **Array** holds.

- Only the top level counts: an element that is itself an array counts as 1.
- Anything that isn't an array, including an object or empty data, counts as 0.
- **Count** updates on the same frame Array changes.

## Tips
- A count wired into a layer's Enabled turns the layer on only while the array has items.
- The last element's position is Count − 1, because positions count from 0.
- To count an object's entries, use Get Keys first. To count a loop, use Loop Count.
patches.behavior:
Stateless.

Each frame:
```
const array = ctx.input("array");
ctx.output("count", Array.isArray(array) ? array.length : 0);
```

- Scope: top-level elements only; nested arrays and objects count as one element each. `null` elements count.
- Non-arrays: objects, text, numbers, booleans, and `null` output 0 without a warning. Text is not measured; that's Text Length.
- Frame 0: evaluates with authored values; no special case.
- Loops: evaluates once per loop index; a loop of arrays gives a loop of counts. It never counts the loop itself.
- Edge cases: the output is always a finite, non-negative integer.
- Coming from Origami: Origami's output is unnamed. Origami doesn't document non-array input; Sonobe outputs 0.

inputs.name: Array
inputs.description: The JSON array to count; anything that isn't an array counts as 0.

outputs.name: Count
outputs.description: The number of top-level elements in Array, 0 or more.

commonMistakes: Count is 0 for data that clearly has items: the data is an object that holds the array, such as {"results": [...]}. Read the array with Value for Key first.
Value at Index with Count shows nothing: positions stop at Count − 1. Subtract 1 to reach the last element.

patches.name: Array Join
patches.summary: Joins several JSON arrays end to end into one array, such as pinned posts followed by the feed.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Array Join puts arrays one after another to make a single array.

- **Array 1**, **Array 2**, and so on are joined in order: every element of Array 1, then every element of Array 2. Change the number of inputs to add more.
- Nothing is removed or reordered, and nested arrays stay nested.
- An input that holds a single value instead of an array, such as one object, is added as one element. Empty inputs add nothing.
- **Array** is the joined result, updated on the same frame any input changes.

## Tips
- Show pinned items first by putting them in Array 1.
- To add one item when someone taps, Array Append remembers each addition.
- The joined array holds up to 10,000 elements.

outputs.name: Array
outputs.description: Every element of the inputs, in port order, as one JSON array.

variadic.name: Array
variadic.description: An array whose elements come after those of the earlier inputs.

commonMistakes: The joined array has only two elements, each a whole list: the inputs are objects that contain arrays, such as {"items": [...]}. Read each array with Value for Key before joining.
The items appear in the wrong order: inputs join from top to bottom. Swap the wires, or reorder the ports.

patches.name: Array Reverse
patches.summary: Outputs a JSON array's elements in the opposite order, like showing the newest message first.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Array Reverse gives back **Array** with its elements in reverse order: the last element becomes the first.

- Only the top level is reversed; arrays inside elements keep their own order.
- Anything that isn't an array gives an empty array.
- **Output** updates on the same frame Array changes.

## Tips
- Lists built with Array Append are oldest first. Reverse them to show the newest item on top.
- To reverse a loop instead of an array, use Loop Reverse.
- For largest-to-smallest order, Array Sort with Descending is more direct.

inputs.name: Array
inputs.description: The JSON array to reverse.

outputs.name: Output
outputs.description: A copy of Array with its elements in reverse order.

commonMistakes: Nothing changes on screen: the list is a loop, not a JSON array. Use Loop Reverse, or reverse the array before Loop Over Array.
Output is empty: Array holds an object that contains the list. Read the list with Value for Key first.

patches.name: Array Sort
patches.summary: Sorts a JSON array from smallest to largest or the reverse, optionally by a field such as price or name.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Array Sort outputs **Array** in order.

- **Sort By** chooses **Ascending** (smallest first, A to Z) or **Descending** (largest first, Z to A).
- **Key** sorts objects by one of their fields, such as `price`. Leave it empty to sort the elements themselves. Elements without that field go last.
- Numbers sort by value. Text sorts alphabetically, ignoring capital letters first, so "apple" comes before "Banana".
- When elements tie, they keep their original order.
- Mixed kinds sort as: empty values, booleans, numbers, text, arrays, then objects.

**Output** is the sorted copy, updated on the same frame any input changes.

## Tips
- Top score: sort Descending by `score`, then Value at Index 0.
- Get Keys, then Array Sort, gives an object's keys in alphabetical order.
- Text such as "10" sorts as text, after "1" and before "2". Store numbers as numbers to sort them by value.

inputs.name: Array
inputs.description: The JSON array to sort.

inputs.name: Sort By

enumOptions.name: Ascending
enumOptions.description: Smallest first: 1, 2, 3 and A to Z.

enumOptions.name: Descending
enumOptions.description: Largest first: 3, 2, 1 and Z to A.

inputs.description: Which direction to sort.

inputs.name: Key
inputs.description: A field to sort objects by, such as price; empty sorts the elements themselves.

outputs.name: Output
outputs.description: A sorted copy of Array.

commonMistakes: Objects don't move: they're compared as ties when Key is empty. Set Key to the field to sort by, such as `name`.
"10" sorts before "9": the numbers are stored as text, which sorts letter by letter. Store them as numbers in the data.
Some items end up at the bottom no matter the direction: they don't have the Key field. Check the field name's spelling and capitals.

patches.name: Array Index Of
patches.summary: Finds where an item sits in a JSON array and whether it's there at all, such as checking if a post is saved.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Array Index Of looks for **Item** in **Array**, starting from the first element.

- **Index** is the position of the first match, counted from 0. It's −1 when Item isn't in the array.
- **Contains** is true when Item is in the array.

Matching is exact. Text must match including capital letters and spaces, and the number 3 doesn't match the text "3". Objects match when they have the same keys and values in any order; arrays match element by element. Colors are compared as `"#RRGGBBAA"` text.

Change the patch's type to match the kind of value in the array.

## Tips
- Wire Contains into an Option Picker to show a filled or outlined icon.
- With a looped Item, each row learns whether it's selected.
- Pair it with Array Append to track saved or selected ids.

inputs.name: Array
inputs.description: The JSON array to search.

inputs.name: Item
inputs.description: The value to look for; it must match an element exactly. Its type follows the patch's type.

outputs.name: Index
outputs.description: The position of the first matching element, counted from 0, or −1 when there's no match.

outputs.name: Contains
outputs.description: True when Item is in Array.

commonMistakes: Contains stays false even though the id is in the list: the list stores numbers and Item is text, or the other way around. Change the patch's type to match the data.
The first row looks selected when nothing is: Index is −1, and index inputs such as Option Picker's Option clamp −1 to 0. Use Contains to decide whether there's a match.

patches.name: Subarray
patches.summary: Takes a run of elements from a JSON array, such as the first five results or one page of a feed.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Subarray copies part of **Array**.

- **Start** is the position of the first element to take, counted from 0.
- **Length** is how many elements to take.
- **Output** holds the elements from Start onward, up to Length of them.

It never fails: if fewer elements remain, you get what's there, and a Start past the end or a Length of 0 gives an empty array. Fractions round down.

## Tips
- Show the top results: Start 0, Length 5.
- Page through a feed: set Start to the page number times the page size, and Length to the page size.
- Array Count on the output tells you how many elements you actually got.
patches.behavior:
Stateless.

Helper: `whole(x) = Number.isFinite(x) ? Math.floor(x + 1e-6) : 0` (the epsilon keeps float results such as 4.9999999999999996 at 5).

Each frame:
```
const array = ctx.input("array");
if (!Array.isArray(array)) { if (array !== null) warnOnce("Array isn't a JSON array, so Subarray outputs []"); ctx.output("output", []); return; }
const start = Math.max(0, whole(ctx.input<number>("start")));
const length = whole(ctx.input<number>("length"));
ctx.output("output", length <= 0 || start >= array.length ? [] : array.slice(start, Math.min(array.length, start + length)));
```

- Ranges: Start is clamped to 0 or more (the `index` port already floors and clamps); Length ≤ 0 or non-finite gives `[]`; Start + Length past the end is cut at the end. Negative Start never counts from the end (CONVENTIONS.md §18.5.9).
- Immutability: a new array every frame; elements are copied by reference.
- Non-arrays: `null` outputs `[]` silently; other values output `[]` and warn once per restart per loop index through `ctx.services.log("warn", …)`.
- Frame 0: evaluates with authored values; no special case.
- Loops: evaluates once per loop index. Looped Start values over one array give a loop of pages. Longest input wins, shorter loops wrap, scalars broadcast.
- Restart and dispose: restart clears the warn-once flag. Nothing to release.
- Coming from Origami: Origami calls Start "Location" and leaves the output unnamed. Origami doesn't document out-of-range ranges; Sonobe clamps like `Array.prototype.slice`.

inputs.name: Array
inputs.description: The JSON array to take elements from.

inputs.name: Start
inputs.description: Position of the first element to take, counted from 0; past the end gives an empty array.

inputs.name: Length
inputs.description: How many elements to take; 0 gives an empty array, and extra length stops at the end.

outputs.name: Output
outputs.description: Up to Length elements of Array, beginning at Start.

commonMistakes: The first result is missing: Start counts from 0. Use Start 0 to begin with the first element.
The last page shows fewer items than expected and nothing breaks: Subarray stops at the end of the array. Use Array Count on the output to hide an empty Next button.

patches.name: JSON to Text
patches.summary: Turns any JSON value into readable JSON text, for checking data on screen or sending it as a message.
patches.docs:
## How it works
JSON to Text writes a JSON value out as text, so you can see what's inside it.

- **JSON** is the value to write out: an object, an array, or a single value.
- **Pretty** puts each entry on its own line, indented by two spaces. Turn it off for compact one-line text, which is better for sending data.
- **Text** is valid JSON text. Text values come out in quotes, and empty data comes out as `null`.

Keys keep the order they have in the object, except that keys made only of digits come first. Colors appear as `"#RRGGBBAA"` text.

## Tips
- Wire a network response into JSON to Text and then into a Text layer to see its structure while you build.
- Text to JSON reads the text back into data.
- Very large responses make long text. Narrow them first with Value for Key or Subarray.

## Coming from Origami
Formerly called Text from JSON. Pretty is a Sonobe addition.

inputs.name: JSON
inputs.description: The object, array, or single value to write out as text.

inputs.name: Pretty
inputs.description: When on, writes one entry per line with 2-space indentation; when off, writes compact one-line text.

outputs.name: Text
outputs.description: The value as JSON text.

commonMistakes: The Text layer shows `null`: the request hasn't returned yet, or the wire comes from the wrong output. Wait for Loading to turn off, and wire the request's Result.
Only part of the text fits on screen: pretty printing adds many lines. Turn Pretty off, make the Text layer taller, or narrow the data with Value for Key first.

patches.name: Text to JSON
patches.summary: Reads text written in JSON format and turns it into data the JSON patches can use.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Text to JSON reads text such as `{"name": "Ada"}` or `[1, 2, 3]` and outputs it as JSON data.

- **Text** is the JSON-formatted text to read. It must be standard JSON: keys and text in double quotes, no trailing commas, no comments.
- **JSON** is the result. It can be an object, an array, or a single value such as a number.
- **Error** turns on when the text isn't valid JSON, and **Error Message** explains why. While there's an error, JSON is empty.
- Empty text, or text with only spaces, gives empty JSON without an error.

## Tips
- Use it on text that holds data, such as a WebSocket message or text from a script.
- JSON to Text does the reverse.
- Show Error Message in a Text layer while you debug a payload.

inputs.name: Text
inputs.description: JSON-formatted text to read; empty text gives empty JSON.

outputs.name: JSON
outputs.description: The data the text describes, or empty when the text is empty or invalid.

outputs.name: Error
outputs.description: True when Text isn't valid JSON.

outputs.name: Error Message
outputs.description: Why the text couldn't be read, or empty text when there's no error.

commonMistakes: Error turns on for text that looks fine: it uses single quotes, unquoted keys, or a trailing comma. Write keys and text in double quotes and remove the last comma.
JSON is empty but Error is off: the text is empty or only spaces. Check that the upstream text has arrived.

patches.name: JSON File
patches.summary: Loads a JSON file from your project, such as a product list or mock feed, so prototypes work without a server.
patches.docs:
## How it works
JSON File reads a `.json` file stored in your project and outputs its contents as data.

- Drop a `.json` file onto the patch editor to create the patch, or choose the file in the inspector. The file lives in the project's assets, so it travels with the prototype.
- **JSON** is the file's data: usually an object or an array.
- **Loading** is true while the file is being read. It usually lasts a frame or two when the prototype starts.
- **Error** turns on when the file is missing or isn't valid JSON, and **Error Message** explains why.

When you replace the file, the patch reads it again. The previous data stays on screen until the new data is ready.

## Tips
- Use a JSON File as mock data while you design, then swap in a Network Request with the same shape.
- Read fields with Value for Key or Value at Path, and make rows with Loop Over Array.
- Keep files small. Very large files slow down loading.

## Coming from Origami
Formerly called Data File.

outputs.name: JSON
outputs.description: The file's contents as data; empty until the file has loaded, and while there's an error.

outputs.name: Loading
outputs.description: True while the file is being read.

outputs.name: Error
outputs.description: True when the file is missing, can't be read, or isn't valid JSON.

outputs.name: Error Message
outputs.description: Why the file couldn't be loaded, or empty text when there's no error.

settings.name: File
settings.description: The id of a JSON file in the project's assets. Drop a .json file on the patch editor to add one.

commonMistakes: Error Message says the file isn't valid JSON: the file has comments, trailing commas, or single quotes. Fix it in a text editor and replace the asset.
The first frame shows empty rows or placeholder text: the file is still loading. Wire Loading into a placeholder's Enabled, or hide the list until JSON arrives.
